title: Blending malt and grain whiskies | Craft Beer School
desc: How malt and grain whiskies differ, why blenders combine them and how a small distillery can approach its first blend.
teaser: Most whisky drunk around the world is a blend. Here is what goes into one and how blenders decide the mix.
standfirst: Blended whisky marries the character of malt whisky with the lightness of grain whisky. It is the style most of the world drinks. It is also harder to make well than it looks. Here is how the two parts differ and how a blender puts them together.
sections:
Malt whisky is made from malted barley, usually in copper pot stills, then distilled to a relatively low strength. It keeps a lot of flavour from the grain, the yeast and the still. Grain whisky is made from cereals such as wheat or maize, with some malted barley for enzymes, then distilled in a continuous column still to a much higher strength. It is lighter, sweeter and softer.

Scotch grain whisky must be distilled to less than 94.8% ABV, so it keeps some character from its raw material. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky sets out the categories.

Malt alone can be intense, variable and expensive. Grain alone can be light and simple. Together, grain carries malt's flavour and smooths its edges while malt gives grain depth. A blend also gives a brand consistency. A blender can draw on many casks and many distilleries to make the same flavour year after year, even as individual casks vary.

The continuous column still, developed in the 19th century and best known in the form patented by Aeneas Coffey in 1830, made grain whisky cheap enough for blending to grow into the main style.

There is no fixed rule. Blends range from a small share of malt to a majority, depending on the style and the price point. A higher malt share usually gives more body and character. A lower share gives a lighter, easier style. The age statement on a blend refers to the youngest whisky in it, malt or grain.

For a craft distillery the ratio is often set by stock. If you make malt and buy in grain, your malt is the scarce component and you plan around it.

Bought-in grain whisky also varies. Ask your supplier for the cereal, the still type, the age and the cask history of each lot. Grain matured in first-fill ex-bourbon casks brings much more vanilla and sweetness to a blend than grain from tired refill casks.
Building a blend in the lab

Blenders work in small volumes before committing casks. A typical approach:

  1. Nose and taste each component cask sample, diluted to around 20% ABV.
  2. Decide what the blend needs: body, fruit, smoke, sweetness, wood.
  3. Make small trial blends in measuring cylinders, for example 30, 40 and 50% malt.
  4. Dilute each trial to the same strength and nose them blind.
  5. Pick one, then refine with small additions of character casks.

Record every trial precisely, in millilitres and strength, so the chosen blend can be scaled to thousands of litres. A blend that cannot be scaled from the notes was a lucky accident.

Work in litres of pure alcohol (LPA), not bulk litres, because components arrive at different strengths. An illustrative example: a blend needs 400 LPA at 40% malt by alcohol. That is 160 LPA of malt and 240 LPA of grain. If the malt is at 60% ABV, you need 266.7 bulk litres of it. If the grain is at 65% ABV, you need 369.2 bulk litres. Reduction water comes later, calculated from the combined strength.

Getting this right matters for cost and for excise records, which in India are kept in alcohol terms. Rules vary by state and change, so check the current notification.

In India, many mainstream whiskies are blends of malt spirit with neutral spirit made from molasses or grain, rather than with grain whisky matured in oak. Rules on what can be called whisky differ between India and markets such as the UK and EU, where whisky must be distilled from cereals and matured in wood. Our guide to molasses versus grain spirit in India explains the difference and why it matters for export.

For a craft distillery aiming at export or premium positioning, the choice of base spirit is a strategic decision, not only a cost one.

Whatever the base, the blending discipline is the same: known components, measured trials and written records that can be repeated.

Freshly combined components often taste disjointed for a while. Most blenders rest the blend before reduction and bottling so the parts settle together. This is called marrying. Our guide to vatting and marrying covers how long and in what vessel. Reduction to bottling strength is then done in stages with clean, low-mineral water.

Getting a blend that tastes the same every year, from casks that never taste the same, is the blender's real job. It takes practice with real samples, not a recipe.
Make three trial blends this week

Take one malt sample and one grain sample. Make three 100 millilitre trials at 20, 40 and 60% malt by alcohol, dilute all three to the same strength and nose them blind with a colleague. Write down which you prefer and why. That small exercise is the start of a blending notebook every distillery should keep.
faqs: What is the difference between malt and grain whisky?
Malt whisky is made from malted barley in pot stills and keeps more flavour. Grain whisky is made from other cereals in column stills at higher strength and is lighter.
What does the age on a blended whisky mean?
It is the age of the youngest whisky in the blend, whether malt or grain.
Why calculate blends in litres of pure alcohol?
Components arrive at different strengths, so working in LPA keeps the proportions and the excise records correct.
